title: POC traffic profiling + quantile/SLA gating - SableWare kickoff
summary: Kickoff for POC to characterize traffic shape and define SLA gating. Agreed on success criteria (95th/99th latency goals, throughput target 180 QPS steady, burst to 450 QPS), dataset/examples for bench, private vs hosted constraints, and 3-week timeline to baseline benchmarks. Action items: send benchmark harness, security checklist, and pilot pricing. Plan for quantile-based assertions and tail latency isolation tests.
topics: Success criteria and gating (p95/p99, error budget)
Workload sizing: QPS, concurrency, burst patterns
Input/output token distribution and batching impact
Benchmark plan & quantile tests (warm KV cache vs cold)
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private network constraints
Timeline and next steps for pilot
action_items: Samir Patel: Share POC commercial worksheet (hosted vs dedicated pricing + burst credits) by 2027-11-12
Jules Harper: Provide benchmark harness repo link + runbook (includes load-pattern scripts and token distribution templates) by 2027-11-10
Priya Nair / SableWare: Share representative prompt set and sample telemetry (1 week of anonymized traffic) by 2027-11-11
Diego Ramos: Confirm network egress rules for Private deployment, and whether we can open test endpoints from SableWare infra by 2027-11-15
next_steps: Schedule 1-hour benchmark run with SableWare test creds (week of 2027-11-15)
Redwood to prepare quantile SLA doc describing p95/p99 measurement methodology and KV-cache warm vs cold scenarios
Customer to decide hosted vs dedicated pilot scope after cost worksheet
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-08
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Jules (Redwood SE), Maya (SableWare VP Eng), Diego (SRE), Priya (ML Eng)
Shared links: Redwood POC workbook (link), benchmark harness repo (link), security checklist (link)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Samir from Redwood here, I'm the AE on the account. Jules, our SE, is with me. How's everybody?
[00:07] Maya: Hey Samir, hi Jules. Maya here. Good, thanks. Die-- Diego and Priya are on as well.
[00:12] Diego: Hey all.
[00:13] Priya: Hi.
[00:15] Samir: Great. We're aiming to scope a short POC to characterize SableWare's production traffic so we can size the pilot and set clear SLA gating. High level, want to confirm success criteria, workload shape, and timeline. Does that sound right to you all?
[00:28] Maya: Yep. We want to know if Redwood can meet our latency goals under our bursty traffic and what the cost profile looks like. Our product has spikes during checkout windows and chat sessions — bursts are the main worry.
[00:38] Jules: Totally understandable. Can you give us rough numbers? Average QPS, peak bursts, average tokens? Even ballpark helps us pick the right test mix.
[00:48] Priya: On average, steady-state is about 180 QPS across the cluster for inference requests. Concurrency per instance varies, but customer-facing flows usually create 8-12 concurrent streams per pod. The bad windows — promo bursts — we've seen short spikes up to roughly 420–480 QPS for a minute or two.
[01:06] Diego: And token counts vary a lot. Typical prompt inputs are 40–90 input tokens; responses average 160 tokens, but full-context threads can push outputs to 400 tokens sometimes.
[01:17] Samir: Good, that helps. So for the POC we'll want to model steady 180 QPS, and replay burst windows of 450 QPS with the long tail where 5–10% of requests go to 300–400 output tokens. We'll include cold and warm KV-cache cases.
[01:33] Maya: Right. Also our SLOs are pretty tight — p95 under 350ms, p99 under 700ms for end-to-end generation when using our standard model config. We understand p99 is harder during cold cache or large outputs.
[01:45] Jules: Quick clarification: are those latency SLOs measured client-side (end-to-end) or server-side token stream timing? Because that'll affect what we assert in the benchmark.
[01:55] Maya: Client-side. Time from request to final token.
[01:57] Samir: Okay, client-side. We'll design the harness to measure end-to-end latencies and produce p50/p90/p95/p99 quantiles plus tail distributions. We'll also instrument tokenization and per-token generation timing.
[02:11] Priya: We should throw in some multi-turn chat sessions — like 6–8 round trips — to see how KV cache growth affects latency and memory.
[02:18] Jules: Yes. For cache effects we'll run warm runs (with pre-populated KV state) and cold runs. We'll also track GPU memory and NVMe eviction metrics.
[02:26] Diego: Network egress: if we run a Private deployment, we need to know if Redwood needs to open public endpoints or if you can host under our VPC peering. Our security team prefers VPC peering; we can't open broad egress.
[02:38] Samir: Noted. For Private we support VPC-based deployments, we won't require broad public egress. We'll document exact port/IP needs in the security checklist.
[02:45] Maya: Great. Also, can you clarify dedicated vs hosted for the pilot — cost-wise, and whether we can start hosted and transition to dedicated?
[02:54] Samir: Yes. We usually recommend starting hosted to iterate quickly, but for strict isolation and predictable throughput dedicated is better. The POC can include both: a short hosted baseline, then a dedicated run for SLA confirmation. We'll include pricing for both in the deck.
[03:11] Jules: For the benchmark harness, the key knobs are QPS shape (steady, burst spike, poisson/randomized), token size distribution, and concurrency per client. We'll provide a JMeter/Locust template plus a Python playback harness that can inject per-request token length distributions.
[03:28] Priya: That sounds perfect. Can you also capture per-route token cost and per-route latency? We have different routes (recommendations, chat, summarization) with different token mixes.
[03:38] Jules: Absolutely. We'll allow you to map route names to token distribution files so each route gets its own latency/cost report.
[03:45] Maya: On acceptance criteria, aside from p95/p99, we want clear regression detection: if p99 increases by more than 25% vs baseline in the dedicated run, that's a fail and we should investigate model variant or batching changes.
[03:58] Samir: We can add automated regression flags in the benchmark report — a pass/fail for quantiles and comparative charts. We'll also surface cost per 1M tokens and cost under steady and burst conditions.
[04:09] Diego: How do you simulate KV cache hit rates? Our workload has ~60% cache hits on average, but when a new product launches it's near zero.
[04:19] Jules: We support configurable cache hit probability in the harness. We can model session stickiness so that repeat user flows hit cache more often. We'll run a matrix: 0%, 60%, 95% hit rates.
[04:29] Priya: For the long outputs, token generation time dominates. Do you support token-level streaming metrics?
[04:35] Jules: Yes — we capture per-token deltas, so we can compute bursty token emission and the token-per-second throughput for the model.
[04:40] Maya: On timeline — what's realistic? We want a bench run and report within three weeks.
[04:45] Samir: That's doable. Proposed schedule: this week — exchange prompt set and test creds; week of 11/15 — run hosted baseline and quantify metrics; week of 11/22 — dedicated run (if requested) and final report by 11/24. Does that align?
[05:00] Maya: Yes. Diego, any red flags?
[05:03] Diego: The only constraint is our security review window. If we go hosted, minimal. If we open a private peering, our infra team needs two business days to configure peering and open endpoints. So plan accordingly.
[05:15] Samir: We'll note that. We'll provide an explicit network runbook for peering.
[05:19] Priya: One more thing — our recent in-house tests showed a token skew distribution where 12% of requests produce >350 tokens. That skew is the main driver of p99. Can you make sure the harness reproduces that tail?
[05:31] Jules: We'll add a heavy-tail distribution to match that 12% > 350 tokens, and also a bimodal distribution for summarization vs chat.
[05:38] Maya: Also curious about batching. Do you recommend batching in production given our low-latency SLOs? Batching reduces cost but can increase tail latency.
[05:47] Samir: Right — it's a tradeoff. Redwood Optimize will give batch-size recommendations. For the POC we can test three modes: no batching (low latency), small batching (tradeoff), and aggressive batching (cost optimized). We'll report delta in p95/p99 and cost per 1M tokens for each.
[06:03] Diego: Will the harness emulate client-side timeouts? Because some of our clients abort after 500ms.
[06:09] Jules: Yes, we include client-level timeouts so you can measure effective success rate under your real client behavior.
[06:14] Priya: How do you measure cold-start NVMe eviction impacts?
[06:18] Jules: We'll run cold-start cases that include model warming steps and then subsequent requests; we instrument disk I/O and K/V fetch latencies. We'll capture the delta between cold and warm in the report.
[06:27] Maya: Security: we need SOC2 Type II evidence and our legal team will want to see data retention and deletion policies.
[06:34] Samir: We'll share our SOC2 summary and the security checklist. For PII handling in prompts, we can enable redaction options or recommend private deployment if regulatory constraints require.
[06:45] Priya: Can we simulate mixed model variants? We sometimes fallback to a cheaper model for low-priority requests.
[06:50] Jules: Yes, the harness supports routing rules to multiple model endpoints to measure heterogenous fleets and fallback latencies. We'll include a small canary setup in the dedicated run to show graceful degradation.
[07:00] Maya: On metrics, please include tokenized cost breakdown (input vs output), concurrency histograms, and per-GPU utilization.
[07:08] Jules: Noted. We'll attach GPU utilization graphs, per-token cost, and concurrency CDFs to the report.
[07:15] Samir: Any competitors or existing vendor constraints?
[07:18] Maya: We're also evaluating Anthropic for a hosted option and considering keeping everything on our internal cluster. We'll want to compare tail latencies and run cost comparisons.
[07:26] Samir: We'll include a competitive template so you can paste Anthropic/OpenAI numbers and compare apples-to-apples for token price and throughput.
[07:33] Diego: One operational question: if p99 spikes during a promotion, do you support automatic fallback to a cheaper but faster small model?
[07:41] Jules: We can configure routing policies by latency/cost budget that fall back to smaller models or regionally replicated endpoints to reduce latency. The POC can test fallback behavior and failover time.
[07:52] Priya: About instrumentation — do you instrument at token-level and expose traces that we can send to our existing tracing?
[07:58] Samir: Yes, we have tracing hooks and can ship traces to your Zipkin/Datadog ingestion. We'll include a tracing integration runbook.
[08:05] Maya: Let's summarize acceptance criteria so we have a shared definition.
[08:08] Diego: I'll list them and Maya can confirm.
[08:10] Diego: 1) p95 < 350ms, 2) p99 < 700ms under steady 180 QPS with 60% cache hits, 3) During 1-minute burst to 450 QPS, p99 must not exceed 1.2s and error rate <1.5%, 4) Cost per 1M tokens no worse than the attached threshold in the POC worksheet, 5) Passing security checklist for hosted or private.
[08:35] Maya: Yes that's the set. We'll add a clause: if p99 improves by <10% vs our current infra in dedicated run, we consider it neutral; if >10% better, that's a win.
[08:45] Samir: Good, we'll encode those as formal gates in the report.
[08:49] Priya: When you run the baseline, will you also capture warm cache and model quantization impact? We might try a 4-bit quantized variant in dedicated.
[08:57] Jules: We can run quantized variants. We'll include an execution path for int8/4-bit and measure latency/cost tradeoffs. Note that quantization can change output quality slightly — we'll surface quality diffs on a small eval set.
[09:10] Maya: Quality diffs are important. We'll provide evaluation prompts to assess hallucination/fluency across quantized runs.
[09:17] Samir: Great. Anything else?
[09:19] Diego: One more: can Redwood's runtime perform token-level early stopping or streaming partial responses to reduce tail?
[09:26] Jules: Early stopping is supported at the application layer; we can simulate it in the harness and measure effective reduction in p99 and token costs. Streaming is supported and we'll measure stream startup time separately.
[09:36] Maya: Okay, next steps recap?
[09:38] Samir: I'll send POC workbook and pricing by Friday 11/12. Jules will push the harness and runbook by Wednesday 11/10. You (Priya) will share the prompt set and 1 week of anonymized telemetry by Thursday 11/11. Then we'll schedule the hosted baseline run the week of 11/15.
[09:57] Priya: Sounds good.
[09:58] Maya: Agreed.
[10:00] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the links.
[10:04] Diego: Thanks.
[10:06] Jules: Thanks all, talk soon.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript fidelity: Speech recognition occasionally merged speaker turns and garbled some product names (e.g., KV cache spelled as K-V cache, Redwood Optimize mis-transcribed in places). There were minor pauses and crosstalk during the Q&A portion.
